d: Provides an overview of events and a summary of Roblox's built-in events.
h:
Events are occurrences within your game that you can listen for and respond to. Many Roblox services and objects have built-in events that automatically fire in response to specific actions or changes.

For example, a player's Character touching a BasePart automatically fires a Touched event. Each time a player joins your game, the Players.PlayerAdded event fires.

Due to the sheer number of events and client-server architecture, Roblox scripting is often referred to as event-driven. This approach is different from many other game engines, which emphasize running code on a frame-by-frame basis.

You don't have to listen for events or take any action in response to them, but the events are firing and available nevertheless. When you do want to respond to an event, you connect a function to it.

Deferred events can help you ensure more performant and consistent event handling. See here for more information.

Connect functions to events

You connect a function to an event using Connect() to execute code each time the event fires. Most events pass arguments to their connected functions. For example, the BasePart.Touched event passes the object that touched the part (such as a left hand or car wheel), and the Players.PlayerAdded event passes the Player that joined your game.

The following code sample demonstrates how to connect a function named onPartTouched() to the Touched event of a part:

-- Assumes the script is parented to the part
local part = script.Parent

-- The function you want to run
local function onPartTouched(object)
    print("Part was touched by", object:GetFullName())
end

-- Connect the function to the part's Touched event
part.Touched:Connect(onPartTouched)

As a best practice and for optimal performance, it's recommended that you disconnect functions when the connection is no longer needed. Note, however, that this may not always be necessary, as all connections to an object's non-deferred events are automatically disconnected if an object is destroyed.

You can also connect anonymous functions to events when you want to use variables in the parent scope and don't need to use the function elsewhere. For example, this code sample avoids the awkward intermediary function from the similar sample in Services:

local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local SaveManager = require(ReplicatedStorage:WaitForChild("SaveManager"))

local function saveProgress(character)
    local position = character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart").Position
    SaveManager.saveData(character, position)
end

-- Anonymous function that calls saveProgress() when a character is removed
-- from the game (in this case, when the player leaves).
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    player.CharacterRemoving:Connect(saveProgress)
end)

Disconnect functions from events

The Connect() method returns an RBXScriptConnection object. If you connect a function to an event, but don't want to call the function the next time an event fires (such as after some condition is met), disconnect it by calling Disconnect() on the RBXScriptConnection object.

The following code sample shows how to connect and disconnect a function from the Part.Touched event:

local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local part = Workspace.Part
local targetPart = Workspace.TargetPart

-- Declare an empty placeholder variable for the connection
local connection

local function onPartTouched(otherPart)
    if otherPart == targetPart then
        print("The part hit the target!")
        -- Disconnect the connection
        connection:Disconnect()
    end
end

-- Connect the above function to the Touched event
connection = part.Touched:Connect(onPartTouched)

If you only want to connect a function to an event once — that is, only run the function the first time the event fires — use the Once() method as a more convenient alternative to connecting and disconnecting the function.

When Luau destroys an event's object, such as the Player object when a user leaves the game, all of its non-deferred connections disconnect automatically.

Wait for events to fire

If you want a script to yield until a specific event fires, use the Wait() method. This method returns the event's arguments, which you can assign to variables for later use:

local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local part = Workspace.Part
local touchedPart = part.Touched:Wait()
print("The part was touched by", touchedPart:GetFullName())

Other types of events

  • Bindable events let you communicate between scripts on the same side of the client-server boundary.

  • Remote events let you communicate across the client-server boundary.

  • Deferred engine events defer event handlers until certain resumption points.

kid.simple: Events are signals that something just happened, like a player joining or a part being touched. Roblox is 'event-driven', which means most of your code waits for events and then reacts. You hook a function to an event with `:Connect()`, and that function runs every time the event fires. You can also stop listening with `:Disconnect()`, listen just once with `:Once()`, or pause until it happens with `:Wait()`.
kid.analogy: An event is like a doorbell: you do not stand at the door all day, you just wait for the ring, and then you go answer it.
keyPoints: Many objects have built-in events, like `Touched` on parts and `PlayerAdded` on the Players service.
Use `event:Connect(myFunction)` to run `myFunction` every time the event fires.
Most events pass information to your function, like which part touched or which player joined.
You can connect an anonymous function written right inside `Connect(function(...) end)`.
`Connect` returns a connection. Call `connection:Disconnect()` to stop listening.
`event:Once(fn)` runs the function only the first time, then stops automatically.
`event:Wait()` pauses the script until the event fires, then gives back its values.
When an object is destroyed, its (non-deferred) connections are disconnected automatically.

terms.event: A signal that something happened in the game.
terms.fire: When an event happens and tells everyone listening. 'The Touched event fired.'
terms.event-driven: A style where code mostly waits for events and reacts, instead of checking things every frame.
terms.connect: Hook a function to an event so it runs when the event fires.
terms.argument: A piece of information passed into a function, like the `player` who joined.
terms.anonymous function: A function without a name, written right where you use it.
terms.RBXScriptConnection: The object `Connect` gives back. You use it to `Disconnect` later.
terms.disconnect: Stop a function from listening to an event.
terms.yield: Pause the script and wait. `Wait()` yields until the event fires.
terms.parent scope: The code area around your function, whose variables your anonymous function can still use.

example.title: Welcome a player only the first time they touch a pad
example.place: Script inside a Part named WelcomePad in Workspace
example.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local pad = script.Parent

local welcomed = {} -- remembers who we already greeted

pad.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	local character = otherPart.Parent
	local player = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
	if player and not welcomed[player] then
		welcomed[player] = true
		print("Welcome, " .. player.Name .. "!")
	end
end)

-- Forget players who leave, so the table does not grow forever
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
	welcomed[player] = nil
end)
explain: `pad.Touched:Connect(...)` runs our function every time something touches the pad.
The event gives us `otherPart`, the part that touched. For a player, its parent is their character.
`GetPlayerFromCharacter` turns the character into a Player, or gives `nil` if it was not a player.
We use a table to greet each player only once.
We connect to `PlayerRemoving` to clean up the table when players leave.

watchOut: Write `part.Touched:Connect(onTouched)`, not `part.Touched:Connect(onTouched())`. The extra `()` calls the function right away instead of connecting it.
`Touched` can fire many times in a row. Use a cooldown or a table like above to avoid repeats.
Connections you make inside other events (like inside `PlayerAdded`) pile up. Disconnect them when you are done, or use `Once` for one-time actions.
`event:Wait()` stops the rest of the script until the event fires. Do not put it where other code needs to keep running.
